clue.text: Wandering one keen to be a music-maker

parts.note: the Wandering Jew of legend, doomed to roam the earth, so the one who wanders is a Jew
keen and sharp both mean having a fine edge or a quick mind

explanation.surface: A restless traveller longs to take up an instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wandering one' looks like a description of the would-be musician, but it points to the legendary Wandering Jew.
explanation.definitionFit: A jew's harp is a small twanging instrument held against the teeth, so it makes music.

clue.text: Sensible recipients of the spoken word

definitions.text: Sensible recipients of the spoken word

parts.words: Sensible recipients of the spoken word
parts.note: sensible here means capable of sensation, so the recipients are body parts that sense sound

explanation.surface: Level-headed people who listen to what is said.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sensible' means able to feel or perceive, not level-headed.
explanation.definitionFit: The membranes in the ears vibrate with sound, so they receive speech through the sense of hearing.

clue.text: Who winged Becky ? Annie ? .

definitions.note: Annie Oakley, the American exhibition marksman, is an example

parts.note: Becky Sharp is the heroine of Thackeray's Vanity Fair
to wing is to wound by shooting, so one who winged is a shooter

explanation.surface: A question about who wounded Becky, with Annie as a suspect.
explanation.walkthrough: Annie Oakley was a famous Wild West crack shot; Becky Sharp is Thackeray's heroine, so the one who shot her is a 'Sharp shooter'.
explanation.definitionFit: Annie Oakley was a celebrated marksman, an example of an expert with a gun.

clue.text: Country which Neptune took in at last, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the words before it might be arranged differently

explanation.surface: A land that the sea god finally swallowed up, maybe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges the letters of 'in at last'. 'took in' looks like a phrase, but 'in' is part of the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Legend says the island kingdom of Atlantis sank beneath the ocean, Neptune's realm.

clue.text: Figure of Miss Peachum, departed it is said

indicators.note: it is said tells us the words are heard, sounding like a different word

parts.note: Polly Peachum is the heroine of Gay's The Beggar's Opera, and departed means gone

explanation.surface: The shape of a stage heroine who has died, so people say.
explanation.walkthrough: Polly Peachum is the heroine of The Beggar's Opera; 'Polly gone' said quickly gives a word for a figure.
explanation.definitionFit: A polygon is a geometric figure with many straight sides.

clue.text: One of eight made by a batsman

definitions.meaning: the oarsman who sets the rhythm in a rowing eight
a hit of the ball in cricket

explanation.surface: A batsman scores one of eight runs.
explanation.definitionFit: Stroke is the rower nearest the stern who sets the pace, and a cricketer's shot is also called by the same name.

clue.text: Such a customer wasn't born on Monday

definitions.text: Such a customer wasn't born on Monday

parts.words: Such a customer wasn't born on Monday
parts.note: the nursery rhyme says Monday's child is fair of face, so this unpleasant customer has the opposite looks

explanation.surface: A remark about a difficult customer's birthday.
explanation.walkthrough: The rhyme 'Monday's child is fair of face' and the idiom for a nasty type, an '___ customer', meet here.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone not fair of face is unattractive, and an unpleasant, threatening person is called this kind of customer.

clue.text: Support for the polls

parts.note: poll is an old word for the head, so the support is something on which heads rest

explanation.surface: Backing given at an election.
explanation.walkthrough: 'polls' looks like elections, but poll is an old word for the head, as in poll tax, a tax per head.
explanation.definitionFit: A pad on a seat back supports a person's head.

clue.text: Neat language à la carte

definitions.note: describes a dish ordered from the menu, here standing for such a dish

parts.note: neat is an old word for cattle, so a single one is an ox
a tongue is a language, as in one's mother tongue

explanation.surface: Someone orders tidy wording off the restaurant menu.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Neat' seems to mean tidy, but it is the archaic word for cattle, still seen in 'neatsfoot oil'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ox-tongue is a dish found on restaurant menus, chosen item by item.

clue.text: Song for a topless Miss Marten

indicators.note: a topless word loses its top, the first letter of the name Maria

parts.note: Maria Marten was the victim in the notorious Red Barn murder of 1827, a staple of Victorian melodrama

explanation.surface: A tune is wanted for a scantily clad young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Maria Marten, murdered in the Red Barn in Suffolk, was a famous melodrama heroine; 'topless' removes her name's first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An aria is a solo song in an opera.

clue.text: Masterman rich and able to pay cash

parts.note: Masterman Ready is a novel by Captain Marryat, so Masterman's surname is Ready
rich people are moneyed, having plenty of wealth

explanation.surface: A wealthy fellow called Masterman can settle his bills on the spot.
explanation.walkthrough: Masterman Ready (1841) is Captain Marryat's shipwreck story for children; its title character supplies the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone with funds to hand has cash available to settle debts immediately.

clue.text: It's mortifying to dine with Heep

definitions.text: It's mortifying to dine with Heep

parts.words: It's mortifying to dine with Heep
parts.note: Uriah Heep in David Copperfield is always 'umble, so dining with him suggests a humble dish, and the phrase means accepting humiliation

explanation.surface: Someone finds a meal with Dickens's Uriah Heep embarrassing.
explanation.walkthrough: Uriah Heep in Dickens's David Copperfield constantly calls himself 'umble; the idiom means having to admit you were wrong.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to apologise humbly or admit a mistake, a humiliating experience.

clue.text: " — and evening star " (Tennyson)

parts.note: fill the gap in the opening line of Tennyson's poem Crossing the Bar, which pairs the end of day with the evening star

explanation.surface: A quotation from Tennyson missing its first word.
explanation.walkthrough: Tennyson's Crossing the Bar opens with the line the clue quotes; the missing word is the time when the evening star appears.
explanation.definitionFit: The close of daylight, when the evening star first shows, begins Tennyson's line about approaching death.

clue.text: Proposal to open the river

parts.note: overt means open, not hidden
the Ure is a Yorkshire river, a crossword favourite

explanation.surface: A plan is put forward to open a river to traffic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to open the river' reads as one action, but 'open' is an adjective and the Ure is a river in Yorkshire, England.
explanation.definitionFit: An overture is an approach or offer made to start negotiations.

clue.text: Embrace an oriental consort

parts.note: oriental means eastern, abbreviated E
a consort is a husband or wife, a spouse

explanation.surface: Someone hugs a partner from the East.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Embrace' looks like a physical hug, but here it means to adopt or support a cause.
explanation.definitionFit: To espouse a cause is to take it up and support it, as one embraces an idea.

clue.text: Iris for example aiding the star-gazer

definitions.text: Iris for example aiding the star-gazer

parts.words: Iris for example aiding the star-gazer
parts.note: the iris is a part of the eye, and a telescope has a lens part that the astronomer looks through

explanation.surface: A girl named Iris helps an astronomer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Iris' looks like a name, but it is the coloured part of the eye, so a piece of the eye.
explanation.definitionFit: The lens a telescope user looks into is named for the eye, and the iris is literally a part of the eye.

clue.text: Petition from Queer Street? That's odd!

indicators.note: something odd is out of the ordinary, telling us the letters of the word before it are jumbled

explanation.surface: A plea comes from someone in financial trouble, which is strange.
explanation.walkthrough: Queer Street is old British slang for being in debt. 'That's odd' rearranges QUEER into REQUE, before ST.
explanation.definitionFit: A request is a formal asking, which is what a petition is.

clue.text: Positive chap, has time to manoeuvre

indicators.note: to manoeuvre is to shift about, signalling that the letters of the words before are moved around

explanation.surface: A confident fellow has a moment to make his move.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to manoeuvre' rearranges the letters of CHAP and TIME; 'has' only joins them.
explanation.definitionFit: Emphatic means forceful and definite, as a positive statement is.

clue.text: Team builder appears to emulate the Prince of Morocco

definitions.text: Team builder appears to emulate the Prince of Morocco

parts.words: Team builder appears to emulate the Prince of Morocco
parts.note: in The Merchant of Venice the Prince of Morocco must choose one of three caskets, so someone who picks a team is doing the same

explanation.surface: A team manager seems to be copying a Shakespearean prince.
explanation.walkthrough: In Shakespeare's The Merchant of Venice, Portia's suitors, the Prince of Morocco first, each pick one casket; an English sports team is picked by a person of the same title.
explanation.definitionFit: One who chooses players for a team picks, just as Morocco chose the gold casket.

clue.text: Complainant starting his action in August ?

definitions.meaning: a game-bird shooter, as the British grouse season opens on 12 August

explanation.surface: A litigant brings his case in the summer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Complainant' and 'action' suggest a lawsuit. In Britain grouse shooting begins on the Glorious Twelfth, 12 August.
explanation.definitionFit: A grouser is a grumbler, and a hunter of the moorland game bird whose season opens in August might jokingly share the name.

clue.text: Glass sometimes used for a laid breakfast

definitions.text: Glass sometimes used for a laid breakfast

parts.words: Glass sometimes used for a laid breakfast
parts.note: the glass is a small sand-glass rather than a drinking glass, and the breakfast is something laid by a hen and boiled

explanation.surface: A glass appears on a carefully laid breakfast table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'laid breakfast' suggests a table that has been set, but what is laid is a hen's product, timed by a small hourglass.
explanation.definitionFit: A small sand-glass times the boiling of the food a hen lays, often for breakfast.

clue.text: Over-rated young lady

definitions.meaning: a cricket over in which no runs are scored is given this name

explanation.surface: A young woman is thought too highly of.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over-rated' looks like 'too highly valued', but it means an over in cricket rated as one with no runs scored.
explanation.definitionFit: A cricket over with no runs is a maiden over, and a maiden is an unmarried girl.

clue.text: Sort of dash from the beach?

definitions.text: Sort of dash from the beach?

parts.words: Sort of dash from the beach?
parts.note: the dash is a wall rendering of small stones, and the stones come from the seashore

explanation.surface: Someone makes a quick run away from the seaside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dash' suggests a sprint, but it is the rendering on house walls studded with small stones, a common British finish.
explanation.definitionFit: A smooth stone from the shore gives its name to the wall finish of small stones pressed into render.

clue.text: A skeleton is not so dumb

definitions.text: A skeleton is not so dumb

parts.words: A skeleton is not so dumb
parts.note: a skeleton is jointed, or articulated, yet it is also speechless, the opposite of articulate

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that a skeleton is cleverer than it looks.
explanation.walkthrough: A skeleton is in articulated form, its bones jointed, and it also cannot speak; 'dumb' here means unable to speak, not stupid.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone unable to express themselves in words is lacking in fluent speech, as a dumb person is.

clue.text: Mrs Pawnbroker ?

parts.note: a pawnbroker is jokingly called uncle in old slang, so his wife would be the matching female relative

explanation.surface: Asking who the wife of a pawnbroker is.
explanation.walkthrough: In old British slang a pawnbroker is 'uncle', so his wife must be his female counterpart in the family.
explanation.definitionFit: The female counterpart of an uncle, here the pawnbroker's slang title, is an aunt by marriage.

clue.text: The way to encourage the hothead

parts.note: to pat someone on the back is to encourage them
read as the head of hot, its first letter

explanation.surface: The best method of encouraging a fiery-tempered person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hothead' seems to be a rash person, but it means the head, or first letter, of 'hot'.
explanation.definitionFit: A path is a track or route, the way to go.

clue.text: Playwright of "Orbit" and "Nothing for Nothing"?

parts.note: the titles are cryptic rewordings: an orbit is the way of the world, and nothing for nothing is love for love, as in tennis scoring

explanation.surface: A question about who wrote two odd-sounding plays.
explanation.walkthrough: The Way of the World and Love for Love are Restoration comedies; 'love' is nil in tennis, hence 'Nothing for Nothing'.
explanation.definitionFit: William Congreve wrote the Restoration comedies The Way of the World and Love for Love.

clue.text: Coker out to attempt modern science

indicators.note: out signals that the letters of the name before it are put out of order

parts.note: an attempt is a try

explanation.surface: A man named Coker heads off to try his hand at the latest science.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges COKER into ROCKE, then TRY follows.
explanation.definitionFit: The science of rocket propulsion and flight was a new field when this puzzle was set.
